## The tasks

The exercise runs as five numbered tasks. Each says what to do in the workspace and, where it differs, in the deck and the browser lab.

### Task 1 – The setup check

The only aim is to reach the point where a line of R runs and the data are in front of you. *Workspace:* open the workspace folder in your IDE and run `source("R/check_setup.R")`, which prints OK when everything is in place and otherwise says what is missing. *Deck and browser lab:* wait for the engine to finish downloading, then run the setup cell. If your installation will not cooperate, carry on in the deck or in the [browser lab](../../lab.qmd#task-1-setup), which run every later task.

### Task 2 – The data, the estimand and the graph

First, meet the `r format(nrow(housing), big.mark = ",")` emails of `housing_emails.csv` ([codebook](../../data/housing_emails_codebook.md)): who was emailed, which names they received, and what came back. Count the emails that bounced, the replies, and the replies that opened with the name of the sender, for each name.

Second, write the **estimand statement** behind the claim. It says which comparison is made (Hispanic names against which names), which emails are counted (the replies, or every delivered email), and which outcome is compared. The [specification menu](../../menu.qmd) gives the template.

Third, finish the **causal graph**. The name affects whether an official replies, and the reply comes before any greeting. Characteristics of the official that the data do not record, such as workload or habits of writing, affect both whether the official replies and whether a reply opens with a name, and so do characteristics of the community. The graph shows why comparing greetings among the replies conditions on a consequence of the name: it compares only the emails that an official chose to answer, and the name may itself have changed that choice, which the [background page](../../background.qmd#sec-posttreatment) calls post-treatment conditioning. It also shows why counting every delivered email keeps the comparison as randomisation made it. In the workspace, dagitty, the R package for causal graphs, answers the questions put to the graph, and tinyplot draws it. The deck and the browser lab cannot run dagitty, so they print the answers that dagitty gives for the graph with and without the arrow from the name to the greeting, read from a table that the course computed with dagitty.

### Task 3 – The reproduction

Choose one of the five analysts in the table above and reproduce the analysis from the public file of the OAs, `housing_original.csv` ([codebook](../../data/housing_original_codebook.md)). Four of them have a statistic recorded in the robustness study, from the $\chi^2$ test of a two-by-two table that 8PTRZ ran to the logistic regression of three groups with covariates that EWFMI fitted, and all four come out exactly. The robustness study recorded no statistic for P9W8Y, so its likelihood-ratio test of the three groups, $\chi^2$ = `r fmt(an("P9W8Y", "statistic_refit"), 3)` on 2 degrees of freedom, can be run again but cannot be matched against the record. The workspace has all five in its report and in `prep/reproduce_reanalyses.R`, and the deck and the [browser lab](../../lab.qmd#task-3-reproduction) have a few cells for each analyst, one step each. When the facilitator says so, the whole class types the analyst and the value that each person reproduced, and sends them at the same moment.

Then find out why your number is what it is. `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` apply a continuity correction to a two-by-two table unless they are told otherwise, so `correct = FALSE` gives `r fmt(chi_plain, 2)` instead of `r fmt(chi_yates, 3)` for 8PTRZ and `r fmt(prop_plain, 2)` instead of `r fmt(prop_yates, 3)` for 25N5D. The z of EWFMI is positive, where that of UYV3F is negative, because its model takes the Hispanic names as the base group. A reproduction depends on the defaults and the codings of the software as well as on the data and the model.

### Task 4 – The menu

This task is **exploratory**. `try_spec()` takes the five arguments of the curve, `comparison`, `population`, `uncoded`, `model` and `adjust`, each of which defaults to the reference specification, so changing one thing means changing one argument. Try several specifications from the [specification menu](../../menu.qmd), one decision at a time, and note which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. An option that is not on the curve, such as `model = "three_group"`, is refused with the reason given in `menu_options.csv`. `my_experiments()` prints everything you have tried side by side. Then choose the one that you would defend, and `submit_exploration()` sends it to the class chart on the [Class results](../../class-results.qmd) page, where it appears as an open circle.

Nothing in this task is preregistered. You may look, change your mind and try again, and the chart marks the result as exploratory for that reason.

### Task 5 – Declaration and report

Choose **one** specification, one option for each decision, and complete the preregistration block **before you run it**: the claim, your option for each decision, and a sentence, grounded in your causal graph, on why the specification answers the claim. `prereg()` prints the block. `run_spec()` fits the specification that you declared, and `report_result()` sends the declared result to the class chart, where it appears as a filled circle. Then find where your result sits on the curve of `r nrow(curve)` specifications.

Task 4 and Task 5 run the same code. An exploratory specification can have been chosen because of its result and a declared one cannot, and you submit both so that the two sets of class results can be compared.
